Housing repair statistics and your cash plan: a prevalence rate cannot price the bill

Five charts distinguish reported major-repair needs, published confidence intervals and a separately quoted repair bill. Test cost assumptions, monthly saving and the payment date.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a reported repair need from the price and timing of a hypothetical bill

Interactive planning lab

Assumed complete bill after the selected cost stress$14,400
Equal monthly saving needed by the selected date, rounded up to cents$1,900
Unfunded cash at the assumed bill date$2,400

The first two charts are fixed official Canadian Housing Survey estimates for Canada (provinces only), released 21 September 2026 and reviewed 25 October 2026. They do not change with the cash controls. Reported repair needs are not prices, individual future probabilities, engineering inspections or decisions about who must pay. The last three figures use an independently invented quoted cash price, a selected extra-cost assumption, dedicated opening cash and monthly saving. The entire stressed bill is assumed to be incurred and paid once at the end of the selected month, immediately after that month’s saving. This is a cost stress, not unused contingency cash automatically treated as spent in every actual project. Both paths continue saving through the due month. Monetary inputs and the assumed bill are rounded to cents; required equal monthly saving is rounded upward to a cent. No interest, inflation, deposit schedule, grants, insurance proceeds, borrowing, legal liability, contractor-performance or repair-urgency assessment is included. Negative scheduled reserve means missing funding. The example assumes this hypothetical payer has independently established responsibility for the whole bill; reported tenure alone cannot establish that.

The central idea

Reported repair prevalence describes households at a survey date. Funding a specific repair requires an independent price, an established payer and a payment calendar.

01

Begin with what the housing statistic actually measures

In the 2024 Canadian Housing Survey table used here, 7.1% of households in Canada’s provinces reported living in dwellings needing major repairs. The corresponding published estimate is 1,167,100 households. This is a weighted estimate for the survey population, not a count of respondents or an inventory of contractor work orders.

The source table, 46-10-0081-01, distinguishes household percentages from person percentages and separates tenure groups. The charts select households. A household with more members does not become several households in this denominator. The selected geography is explicitly Canada (provinces only), so it should not be relabelled as including the territories.

Dwelling condition is assessed by the respondent. A reported need does not provide a technical inspection, a repair scope, a cash price or a payment deadline. Those missing quantities matter when the question changes from describing housing conditions to deciding how much cash a particular bill requires.

02

Keep survey cycles and condition categories separate

The current 2024 survey release is dated 21 September 2026. This article reviewed the source on 25 October 2026. The history contains four survey reference years: 2018, 2021, 2022 and 2024. The year spacing in the line chart reflects those actual gaps. There is no invented 2019, 2020 or 2023 observation.

Major-repair point estimates are 7.0%, 7.4%, 7.3% and 7.1% across those cycles. The connecting segments help locate the observations; they do not trace the same households over time or estimate the unobserved years. This article makes no independent claim that the small point-estimate changes are statistically significant.

20227.3%6.8%–7.9%

For total tenure in 2024, the three condition percentages are regular maintenance needed 71.0%, minor repairs needed 22.0% and major repairs needed 7.1%. They add to 100.1% because the published figures are rounded independently. Preserve that rounding instead of changing a category to manufacture an exact total.

These condition categories are distinct from housing suitability, which is another dimension in the same table. A dwelling can have a repair issue without the table establishing a household’s affordability or core-housing-need status. This small guide does not combine those separate classifications.

03

Read the respondent-assessment and coverage limits

Table footnote 4 explains that dwelling-condition responses can vary with the time, season and context of assessment. Desirable remodeling and additions are excluded from the repair assessment. The survey category therefore should not be equated with every discretionary renovation someone might want to purchase.

The 2024 Canadian Housing Survey metadata describes its target population and exclusions, including institutional residents, people in Armed Forces camps, reserves and other Indigenous settlements, and specified collective dwellings. The table uses 2021 Census geography boundaries. The national-looking label still needs its survey and geography qualifications.

The owner and renter responses describe reported dwelling condition. They do not establish who owns a damaged component, whether a landlord has an obligation, whether work is urgent, or whether insurance covers it. Those questions depend on the actual property, agreement and applicable process. The hypothetical cash example below assumes that responsibility for its complete bill has already been established separately.

04

Read confidence intervals as uncertainty about estimates

The 2024 all-tenure estimate is 7.1%, with a published 95% confidence interval of 6.6% to 7.7%. Owner households are 6.5%, with 5.8% to 7.3%; renter households are 8.4%, with 7.6% to 9.2%. The interval bars reproduce those published bounds, including their asymmetry.

Each tenure percentage uses households in that tenure group as its denominator. All tenures already includes both owner and renter households. Adding the three percentages or taking their simple average would not describe an overall prevalence. No unweighted calculation is substituted for the published total.

The whiskers express sampling uncertainty around a population estimate. They are not a range within which 95% of an individual property’s repair expenses fall, and they do not estimate the future chance that a particular home needs work. The source rows used here have blank status and symbol fields; that does not mean the estimates have no uncertainty.

Comparing point estimates alone also cannot explain why tenure groups differ. This article does not estimate an effect of renting, test group differences or decide which group should set aside more cash. A repair budget needs evidence specific to the bill, rather than a personal rule inferred from the group label.

05

Use an independent quote rather than multiplying the survey rate by a home value

The cash example starts with an invented quoted price of CAD 12,000, including assumed applicable taxes. It adds an assumed extra cost of 20%, or CAD 2,400, producing a complete stressed bill of CAD 14,400. The survey percentage does not enter this calculation.

A cross-sectional prevalence rate has neither the required personal time horizon nor a repair-cost amount. Multiplying 7.1% by a property value would not supply a quoted repair price or a justified personal reserve. The underlying component, work scope, payer and due date remain unknown from that multiplication.

The selected cost stress assumes the extra amount is actually incurred in that scenario. In a real project, money held as a contingency can remain unspent. The chart therefore calls CAD 14,400 an assumed complete stressed bill, rather than silently treating every contingency allowance as an inevitable expense.

The comparison path pays the original CAD 12,000 quote with no extra cost. Both paths use the same opening cash, monthly saving and bill date. This isolates the funding effect of a changed price assumption; it does not forecast a contractor’s final invoice or the cost of delaying the work.

06

Fund the date on which the entire assumed bill is due

The default plan has CAD 3,000 dedicated to the repair and sets aside CAD 1,500 each month. That opening amount is assigned to this bill and is not simultaneously counted as a separately protected emergency reserve or another goal’s funding. The entire bill is paid at the end of Month 6, immediately after that month’s saving contribution. Six contributions total CAD 9,000, bringing resources before payment to CAD 12,000.

The original quote is exactly funded, leaving zero. The stressed CAD 14,400 bill leaves negative CAD 2,400 of scheduled reserve. That negative point identifies missing funding; the model does not assume an overdraft, unpaid contractor balance or new insurance payment to make it disappear.

For the stressed bill, the additional amount to fund after the opening reserve is CAD 11,400. Dividing by six gives CAD 1,900 per month. The selected CAD 1,500 saving plan is CAD 400 per month lower, producing the CAD 2,400 difference over six months. The three metrics keep the bill amount, required monthly saving and unfunded amount distinct.

The tool rounds monetary inputs and the assumed bill to cents, then rounds required monthly saving upward to a cent. Both plotted paths continue making the entered contribution through the due month, including when opening cash already covers the target. Any excess remains as a positive ending reserve.

A real deposit, progress payment or earlier invoice would require a different calendar. No money is paid before the single modeled bill date. Moving that date changes the funding arithmetic but cannot establish that the work can safely or lawfully wait.

07

Use the matrix to separate the cost assumption from the saving deadline

The matrix keeps the independent quote and dedicated opening cash unchanged. Columns replace the extra-cost assumption with 0%, 10%, 20% or 30%. Rows replace the full-payment date with three, six, twelve or twenty-four months. Each cell is the equal monthly saving required for that separate plan, rounded upward to a cent.

At the default quote and opening reserve, the 20% stress requires CAD 3,800 per month over three months, CAD 1,900 over six, CAD 950 over twelve and CAD 475 over twenty-four. Those differences reflect more saving contributions, with no interest, price growth or change in work scope.

The entered planned monthly saving does not change the matrix because it is an amount to compare with the requirement, rather than a component of the requirement formula. It does change the scheduled-reserve line and the resulting gap. Compact chart labels save space; the expandable table preserves cent amounts.

A longer displayed period is a mathematical comparison. It is not a recommendation to postpone a necessary repair, and it does not include deterioration, temporary accommodation or missed-payment costs. Those facts require their own scope and dated cash plan.

08

Bring the right evidence to each planning question

For the statistic, retain the household denominator, provinces-only geography, condition definition, survey reference year and published interval together. For the bill, establish the work scope, quoted cash price, applicable taxes, payer, payment stages and money already dedicated to it. Population prevalence and a contractor quote supply different evidence.

The model assumes no interest on the reserve, inflation, investment returns, grants, insurance proceeds or borrowing. It makes no repair-urgency or engineering assessment. It also assumes the chosen payer is responsible for the complete hypothetical amount; the owner/renter labels in the survey cannot establish that responsibility.

Once the price and calendar are known, the longer-term replacement-reserve guide can help compare several component dates, while the renovation payment-calendar guide addresses staged payments. Keep those calendars grounded in the project’s own records rather than treating the national repair rate as a funding rule.

Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
